title: Robust quantum state certification and uncertainty principles for total influence
abstract: We show that nonadaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements suffice to test whether an unknown $n$-qubit state $ρ$ is $\varepsilon$-close to or $O(\varepsilon)$-far from an ideal target state $|ψ\rangle$, for all but a $2^{-Ω(n)}$ fraction of target states. The test uses $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/δ))$ copies of $ρ$ to achieve confidence $1-δ$, which is information-theoretically optimal even among protocols with arbitrary joint measurements. The main technical innovation is an uncertainty principle for weighted generalizations of the total influence of Boolean functions. As a simple example, the unweighted variant states that $\mathbf{Inf}[f]+\mathbf{Inf}[\widehat{f}] = Ω(n)$, which is a natural hypercube analogue of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (here $\widehat{\,\cdot\,}$ denotes the $2^{-n/2}$-normalized Fourier transform). The weighted case generalizes $\mathbf{Inf}[\,\cdot\,]$ and $\mathbf{Inf}[\,\widehat{\,\cdot\,}\,]$ to Dirichlet energies associated with Glauber dynamics for certain dual measures on the cube.

bite.hook: Single-qubit Pauli measurements suffice to test almost all n-qubit quantum states with optimal sample efficiency.
tldr: Showed that nonadaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements can test if an unknown state matches a target state for almost all targets.
Proved an uncertainty principle for total influence and Fourier transforms of Boolean functions on hypercubes.
Achieved optimal sample efficiency O(ε⁻² log(1/δ)) matching protocols with arbitrary joint measurements.
bite.whyItMatters: Quantum state certification typically requires complex, multi-qubit joint measurements. Proving simple single-qubit checks are optimal drastically reduces the experimental hardware needed to verify quantum states.
bite.eli5: Checking if a quantum computer created the right complex state is like inspecting a huge building. Instead of needing hyper-advanced scanning machinery, this paper proves you can inspect bricks one by one and still get a near-perfect answer.
